claim: Approximately 80% of targeted CGE-NGFCs (124 out of 150 EGFP-positive INs) displayed late-spiking (LS; with varying degrees of latency) phenotype.
source: Approximately 80% of targeted CGE-NGFCs (124 out of 150 EGFP-positive INs) displayed late-spiking (LS; with varying degrees of latency) phenotype and an axo-dendritic morphology (38 EGFP-positive INs) characteristic of NGFCs (Overstreet-Wadiche and McBain, 2015; Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific numerical data (124 out of 150 cells) from experimental observations.

claim: 38 EGFP-positive INs displayed an axo-dendritic morphology characteristic of NGFCs.
source: Approximately 80% of targeted CGE-NGFCs (124 out of 150 EGFP-positive INs) displayed late-spiking (LS; with varying degrees of latency) phenotype and an axo-dendritic morphology (38 EGFP-positive INs) characteristic of NGFCs (Overstreet-Wadiche and McBain, 2015; Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific numerical data (38 cells) from experimental observations and cites prior work establishing this as characteristic of NGFCs.

claim: Conditioning APs resulted in barrage/persistent firing (BF) in approximately 70% of NGFCs tested (86 out of 124 NGFCs).
source: These conditioning APs resulted in the previously described phenomenon of barrage/persistent firing (BF) (Deemyad et al., 2018; Elgueta et al., 2015; Imbrosci et al., 2015; Jung and Hoffman, 2009; Krook-Magnuson et al., 2011; Rózsa et al., 2017; Sheffield et al., 2011; Suzuki et al., 2014) in approximately 70% of NGFCs tested (86 out of 124 NGFCs; Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific numerical data (86 out of 124 cells) from experimental observations and cites multiple prior studies describing this phenomenon.

claim: BF was elicited in 48% of human NGFCs (12/25 NGFCs tested).
source: Upon delivering the same induction protocol as described above, BF was elicited in 48% of human NGFCs (12/25 NGFCs tested; Figure 1D; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,C).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific numerical data (12 out of 25 cells) from experimental observations on human tissue.

claim: BF could not be elicited in superficial cortical and hippocampal INs that were not NGFCs (non-NGFCs), including the recently described human rosehip cell.
source: Interestingly, even with the number of conditioning APs far exceeding that required to induce BF in NGFCs (800–1500 APs; 30 Hz), BF could not be elicited in superficial cortical and hippocampal INs that were not NGFCs (non-NGFCs), including the recently described human rosehip cell (Boldog et al., 2018) (26 and 37 non-NGFCs tested for BF induction in mouse and human, respectively; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,D).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific numerical data (26 and 37 cells) from experimental observations and cites prior work describing the rosehip cell.

claim: The mean BF duration in human NGFCs was approximately double on average compared to mouse NGFCs.
source: Despite a similar number of conditioning APs necessary for BF induction being similar in both species, the mean BF duration in human NGFCs albeit more variable, was approximately double on average (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: The manuscript states this comparison and references figures showing the data.

claim: NGFCs could not display another bout of BF when the induction protocol was continued immediately following cessation of BF.
source: In some recordings, the induction protocol was continued immediately following cessation of BF to ascertain whether subsequent BF epochs of a longer duration could be triggered. However, NGFCs could not display another bout of BF using this experimental approach (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental observations and references a figure showing this result.

claim: Subsequent BF episodes could be elicited provided a sufficient refractory period had elapsed between delivery of subsequent induction protocols.
source: Interestingly, subsequent BF episodes could be elicited provided a sufficient refractory period had elapsed between delivery of subsequent induction protocols (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental observations and references a figure showing this result.

claim: Multiple BF episodes (up to four were tested) could be reliably triggered when allowing greater than 1 min before subsequent induction delivery.
source: Circumventing such constraints in BF induction (i.e. allowing greater than 1 min before subsequent induction delivery; Figure 1—figure supplement 2C) multiple BF episodes (up to four were tested) could be reliably triggered (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,D,E).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental observations and references figures showing this result.

claim: Spiking events during NGFC BF episodes in mouse and human were comprised of both spikelets and overshooting action potential spikes.
source: Spiking events during NGFC BF episodes in mouse and human were comprised of both spikelets and overshooting action potential spikes (the latter defined as those in which the peak overshot 0 mV; Figure 1B,D,G).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental observations and references figures showing this result.

claim: The spikelet waveform was typically nested within that of the spike as evidenced by a prominent inflection point in the voltage rise of the latter and in corresponding phase plots.
source: The spikelet waveform was typically nested within that of the spike as evidenced by a prominent inflection point in the voltage rise of the latter and in corresponding phase plots (Figure 1G,H).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental observations and references figures showing this result.

claim: BF consists of spontaneous AP originating at very distal axonal site(s) that travel retrogradely towards the soma and in some instances subsequently trigger an AP at more proximal sites.
source: This biphasic rise, noted in previous studies (Elgueta et al., 2015; Sheffield et al., 2011), has led to the notion that BF consists of spontaneous AP originating at very distal axonal site(s) that travel retrogradely towards the soma and in some instances subsequently trigger an AP at more proximal sites (Elgueta et al., 2015; Imbrosci et al., 2015; Sheffield et al., 2011) (hence also referred to as retro-axonal BF Sheffield et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple prior studies that have proposed this mechanism based on the biphasic rise observed.

claim: Of the IN subtypes residing in superficial lamina of cortical and hippocampal microcircuits, NGFCs are privileged with regard an ability to express BF in brief, repeatable episodes.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that, of the IN subtypes residing in superficial lamina of cortical and hippocampal microcircuits, NGFCs are privileged with regard an ability to express BF in brief, repeatable episodes.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes experimental findings showing that NGFCs, but not other INs, can express BF.

claim: Activity-dependent functional plasticity originating in the distal axonal compartments is conserved in NGFCs embedded in human cortical circuits.
source: Furthermore, this activity-dependent functional plasticity originating in the distal axonal compartments, is clearly conserved in NGFCs embedded in human cortical circuits.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes experimental findings showing similar BF in both mouse and human NGFCs.

claim: A leftward shift in the input/output curve and increased total number of action potentials were evident after excursions into the BF mode.
source: A leftward shift in the input/output curve and increased total number of action potentials were evident after excursions into the BF mode (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental observations and references figures showing this result.

claim: The increased excitability observed after BF occurred in the absence of changes in input resistance.
source: The increased excitability observed here occurred in the absence of changes in input resistance (208 ± 53 mΩ and 220 ± 47 mΩ for baseline vs. STP-SE, respectively; n = 11 mouse NGFCs; p=0.33).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific numerical data from experimental measurements with statistical analysis.

claim: The potentiated NGFC output following cessation of BF1 was found to persist for a mean duration of approximately 60 s.
source: Using this approach, the potentiated NGFC output following cessation of BF1 was found to persist for a mean duration of approximately 60 s (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific numerical data from experimental measurements and references figures.

claim: The duration of BFs expressed in individual NGFCs does not increase with repeated induction.
source: Interestingly, even though the duration of BFs expressed in individual NGFCs does not increase with repeated induction (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), the potentiation of somatic depolarization-induced output after the cessation of these subsequent BF episodes was markedly prolonged thus demonstrating the ability to prime this mode of plasticity by multiple rounds of induction (Figure 2G; Note: in three instances after cessation of BF4 heightened action potential output lasted 900 s at which point the experiment was terminated).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental observations and references figures showing this result.

claim: Both mouse and human NGFCs exhibit an activity-dependent increase in the sensitivity to proximal somatic depolarizing stimuli.
source: These data demonstrate that, in addition to the ability to undergo brief periods of distal axonal plasticity (i.e. BF), both mouse and human NGFCs also exhibit an activity-dependent increase in the sensitivity to proximal somatic depolarizing stimuli.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes experimental findings showing increased excitability in both species.

claim: STP-SE was readily elicited in the absence of measurable BF in mouse hippocampal (n = 9) and human cortical NGFCs (n = 4).
source: Notably, with this induction strategy, STP-SE was readily elicited in the absence of measurable BF in mouse hippocampal (n = 9) and human cortical NGFCs (n-4; Figure 3A–D) with the mean number of conditioning APs to elicit potentiation in excitability significantly lower than that required to induce BF (Figure 3E).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific numerical data from experimental observations and references figures.

claim: The mean number of conditioning APs to elicit STP-SE was significantly lower than that required to induce BF.
source: Notably, with this induction strategy, STP-SE was readily elicited in the absence of measurable BF in mouse hippocampal (n = 9) and human cortical NGFCs (n-4; Figure 3A–D) with the mean number of conditioning APs to elicit potentiation in excitability significantly lower than that required to induce BF (Figure 3E).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific numerical data from experimental observations with statistical comparison and references figures.

claim: A subset of NGFCs (7/16 and 2/6 mouse hippocampal and human cortical NGFCs, respectively) were unable to undergo STP-SE even under protracted period of conditioning APs.
source: As with BF, a subset of NGFCs (7/16 and 2/6 mouse hippocampal and human cortical NGFCs, respectively) and non-late spiking INs (4/4 and 3/3 mouse and human non-NGFCs, respectively) were unable to undergo STP-SE even under protracted period of conditioning APs (Figure 3D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific numerical data from experimental observations and references figures.

claim: Non-late spiking INs (4/4 and 3/3 mouse and human non-NGFCs, respectively) were unable to undergo STP-SE even under protracted period of conditioning APs.
source: As with BF, a subset of NGFCs (7/16 and 2/6 mouse hippocampal and human cortical NGFCs, respectively) and non-late spiking INs (4/4 and 3/3 mouse and human non-NGFCs, respectively) were unable to undergo STP-SE even under protracted period of conditioning APs (Figure 3D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific numerical data from experimental observations and references figures.

claim: STP-SE was characterized by a significant hyperpolarization of action potential threshold.
source: Finally, this potentiation of intrinsic excitability was characterized by a significant hyperpolarization of action potential threshold (Figure 3F–H) and reduction in the delay to spiking (Figure 3B,C,I) which in combination likely contributes to STP-SE.
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental observations with statistical analysis and references figures.

claim: STP-SE was characterized by a reduction in the delay to spiking.
source: Finally, this potentiation of intrinsic excitability was characterized by a significant hyperpolarization of action potential threshold (Figure 3F–H) and reduction in the delay to spiking (Figure 3B,C,I) which in combination likely contributes to STP-SE.
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental observations with statistical analysis and references figures.

claim: Both mouse and human NGFCs undergo an activity-dependent potentiation of their action potential output in response to somatic depolarizations without the requirement of entering into BF.
source: Together, these data demonstrate the propensity of both mouse and human NGFCs to undergo an activity-dependent potentiation of their action potential output in response to somatic depolarizations without the requirement of entering into BF.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes experimental findings showing STP-SE can occur independently of BF.

claim: Depolarizing steps from −70 mV to membrane potentials close to AP threshold revealed both inactivating and to a lesser extent sustained K+-conductances operating at subthreshold membrane potentials.
source: Depolarizing steps from −70 mV to membrane potentials close to AP threshold (AP threshold in NGFCs = −29 ± 0.3 mV; n = 70) revealed both inactivating and to a lesser extent sustained K+-conductances operating at subthreshold membrane potentials (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental observations and references figures showing this result.

claim: The subthreshold K+-conductance(s) in NGFCs was not significantly inhibited by α-dendrotoxin (DTX; 100–200 nM).
source: However, the subthreshold K+-conductance(s) in NGFCs was not significantly inhibited by α-dendrotoxin (DTX; 100–200 nM), a specific blocker of Kv1 (Kv1.1, Kv1,2 and Kv1.6) channels (Figure 4D).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental observations with pharmacological manipulation and references figures.

claim: A low concentration of 4-AP (low 4-AP; 100 μM) caused only a modest yet statistically significant inhibition of subthreshold K+-conductance(s).
source: A low concentration of 4-AP (low 4-AP; 100 μM), which also blocks Kv1 channels, caused only a modest yet statistically significant inhibition of subthreshold K+-conductance(s) (Figure 4D).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental observations with pharmacological manipulation and statistical analysis, and references figures.

claim: Millimolar concentrations of 4-AP (high 4-AP; 1–3 mM) produced a significant robust inhibition of the subthreshold K+-conductance.
source: In contrast, millimolar concentrations of 4-AP (high 4-AP; 1–3 mM) produced a significant robust inhibition of the subthreshold K+-conductance with this digitally isolated conductance exhibiting a distinct inactivating time profile reminiscent of A-type K+-channels (IKA; Figure 4D,E).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental observations with pharmacological manipulation and statistical analysis, and references figures.

claim: The digitally isolated conductance inhibited by high 4-AP exhibited a distinct inactivating time profile reminiscent of A-type K+-channels (IKA).
source: In contrast, millimolar concentrations of 4-AP (high 4-AP; 1–3 mM) produced a significant robust inhibition of the subthreshold K+-conductance with this digitally isolated conductance exhibiting a distinct inactivating time profile reminiscent of A-type K+-channels (IKA; Figure 4D,E).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental observations and references figures showing this result.

claim: High 4-AP and 4-AP delivered to NGFCs via the intracellular patch pipette (intra 4-AP; 3 mM) modulated the delay to spike and hyperpolarized the AP threshold to an extent that more closely mimics the shift in both these parameters observed during STP-SE.
source: In contrast, high 4-AP and 4-AP delivered to NGFCs via the intracellular patch pipette (intra 4-AP; 3 mM) (Jung and Hoffman, 2009), modulated the delay to spike and hyperpolarized the AP threshold to an extent that more closely mimics the shift in both these parameters observed during STP-SE (Figure 4G–I).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental observations with pharmacological manipulation and references figures.

claim: DTX and low 4-AP increased intrinsic excitability to a much lesser extent than high 4-AP or intra 4-AP.
source: In agreement with the propensity to modulate spike latency and AP threshold (Figure 4I), DTX and low 4-AP increased intrinsic excitability to a much lesser extent than high 4-AP or intra 4-AP (Figure 5A-C).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental observations with pharmacological manipulation and references figures.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of IKA with millimolar concentrations of 4-AP results in a transformation of the membrane voltage response characterized by the emergence of a depolarizing hump.
source: Interestingly (in the presence of TTX) pharmacological inhibition of IKA with millimolar concentrations of 4-AP results in a transformation of the membrane voltage response characterized by the emergence of a depolarizing hump (Figure 5D) as would be predicted by the time-dependent profile of IKA (Figure 4B, E).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental observations with pharmacological manipulation and references figures.

claim: The time course of the recovery from inactivation of IKA is mirrored by that seen in the recovery of the delay to spike.
source: We reveal that the time course of the recovery from inactivation of IKA is mirrored by that seen in the recovery of the delay to spike (Figure 5G).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental observations and references figures showing this result.

claim: A close relationship exists between the extent of IKA inhibition in NGFCs and corresponding increase in intrinsic excitability as measured by action potential output to the depolarizing test current injection.
source: Furthermore, a close relationship exists between the extent of IKA inhibition in NGFCs (mediated by the differing magnitudes of recovery from inactivation) and corresponding increase in intrinsic excitability as measured by action potential output to the depolarizing test current injection (Figure 5H).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental observations and references figures showing this result.

claim: A transient, subthreshold K+-conductance(s) sensitive to high concentrations of 4-AP is a major contributor in dictating action potential latency, threshold and ultimately intrinsic excitability in NGFCs.
source: Together, these pharmacological/biophysical analyses demonstrate that a transient, subthreshold K+-conductance(s) sensitive to high concentrations of 4-AP is a major contributor in dictating action potential latency, threshold and ultimately intrinsic excitability in NGFCs.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes experimental findings from pharmacological and biophysical analyses.

claim: STP-SE could be induced more readily with 4-AP containing internal solution as indicated by a leftward shift in the time course of potentiation that corresponds to a significant reduction in the number of required conditioning APs.
source: Interleaved experiments (K-gluconate control vs. K-gluconate with intra 4-AP) clearly demonstrate that STP-SE could be induced more readily 4-AP containing internal solution as indicated by a leftward shift in the time course of potentiation that corresponds to a significant reduction in the number of required conditioning APs (Figure 5I,J).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental observations with statistical analysis and references figures.

claim: The gain of function with intra-4-AP provides further evidence for a reduction in 4-AP sensitive conductance(s) particularly those that resemble IKA, as a contributing factor in STP-SE.
source: This gain of function provides further evidence for a reduction in 4-AP sensitive conductance(s) particularly those that resemble IKA, as a contributing factor in STP-SE.
evidence: The manuscript interprets experimental findings to support a mechanistic role for IKA in STP-SE.

claim: Due to the inability to fully occlude STP-SE with intra-4-AP, a role for additional modulation of other channels that are insensitive to intra-4-AP block cannot be ruled out.
source: However, due to our inability to fully occlude STP-SE we cannot rule out a role for additional modulation of other channels that are insensitive to intra-4-AP block.
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges limitations in the experimental findings and speculates about alternative mechanisms.

claim: CGE-NGFCs possess essentially no mRNA encoding for Kv1.4 (Kcna4), Kv3.3 (Kcnc3) and Kv4.1 (Kcnd1) subunits.
source: Focusing attention on the 3626 neurons within the cluster corresponding to cortical and hippocampal CGE-NGFCs (Figure 6A; Figure 6—figure supplement 1C; see Materials and methods for details) these analyses reveal that essentially no mRNA encoding for Kv1.4 (Kcna4), Kv3.3 (Kcnc3) and Kv4.1 (Kcnd1) subunits indicating their unlikely contribution to IKA in CGE-NGFCs (Figure 6B).
evidence: The manuscript describes analysis of publicly available RNAseq data and references figures.

claim: CGE-NGFCs possess appreciable mRNA levels of Kcnc4, Kcnd2 and Kcnd3 mRNA that encode for Kv3.4, Kv4.2 and Kv4.3 subunits, respectively.
source: In contrast, appreciable mRNA levels of Kcnc4, Kcnd2 and Kcnd3 mRNA that encode for Kv3.4, Kv4.2 and Kv4.3 subunits, respectively, were apparent (Figure 6B).
evidence: The manuscript describes analysis of publicly available RNAseq data and references figures.

claim: IKA in NGFCs is TEA insensitive indicating that Kv3.4 does not appreciably mediate NGFC IKA.
source: As expected, TEA at the concentrations used (2–10 mM) reliably inhibits IKDR (Figure 6C,D). However, IKA in NGFCs is TEA insensitive indicating that Kv3.4 does not appreciably mediate NGFC IKA (Rudy and McBain, 2001) despite the presence of detectable levels of mRNA (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental observations with pharmacological manipulation and references figures, and cites prior work on TEA sensitivity.

claim: IKA is largely abolished by the selective Kv4 blocker, AmmTx3 (% baseline IKA peak after 200 nM AmmTx3 = 29.6 ± 9.9%; n = 4).
source: In contrast, IKA is largely abolished by the selective Kv4 blocker, AmmTx3 (Maffie et al., 2013) (% baseline IKA peak after 200 nM AmmTx3 = 29.6 ± 9.9%; n = 4; Figure 6C,D).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental observations with pharmacological manipulation, provides specific numerical data, and references figures and prior work.

claim: Kcnd2/Kv4.2 is predominantly expressed in PCs, particularly those in the CA1 region.
source: In general, Kcnd2/Kv4.2 is predominantly expressed in PCs, particularly those in the CA1 region (Figure 6E,F; see Materials and methods for details), whereas Kcnd3/Kv4.3 is mainly restricted to INs (Lien et al., 2002; Menegola et al., 2008; Rhodes et al., 2004; Serôdio and Rudy, 1998).
evidence: The manuscript describes analysis of RNAseq data and in situ hybridization, references figures, and cites prior work.

claim: Kcnd3/Kv4.3 is mainly restricted to INs.
source: In general, Kcnd2/Kv4.2 is predominantly expressed in PCs, particularly those in the CA1 region (Figure 6E,F; see Materials and methods for details), whereas Kcnd3/Kv4.3 is mainly restricted to INs (Lien et al., 2002; Menegola et al., 2008; Rhodes et al., 2004; Serôdio and Rudy, 1998).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple prior studies establishing this expression pattern.

claim: NGFCs possess comparable levels of combined mRNA encoding Kcnd2 and Kcnd3 to that seen in PCs.
source: Here, the molecular profile analyses demonstrate that at least at the transcript level revealed by RNAseq analyses, NGFCs possess comparable levels of combined mRNA encoding Kcnd2 and Kcnd3 to that seen in PCs (Figure 6E).
evidence: The manuscript describes analysis of RNAseq data and references figures.

claim: In situ hybridization using the RNAscope platform revealed the presence of detectable Kcnd2 and Kcnd3 mRNA in putative SLM hippocampal NGFCs (identified by NDNF mRNA expression).
source: In agreement with the RNAseq and functional data, in situ hybridization using the RNAscope platform (see Materials and methods for details) revealed the presence of detectable Kcnd2 and Kcnd3 mRNA in putative SLM hippocampal NGFCs (identified by NDNF mRNA expression; Figure 6G–I).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental observations using in situ hybridization and references figures.

claim: Expression of mRNA for well-known Kv4 auxiliary subunits KChIPs and DPLPs in NGFCs (particularly Kcnip1, Kcnip4, Dpp6 and Dpp10) is essentially similar if not higher to that observed in hippocampal pyramidal cells.
source: Finally, expression of mRNA for well-known Kv4 auxiliary subunits KChIPs and DPLPs in NGFCs (particularly Kcnip1, Kcnip4, Dpp6 and Dpp10) albeit with a differential complement, is essentially similar if not higher to that observed in hippocampal pyramidal cells (Figure 6J).
evidence: The manuscript describes analysis of RNAseq data and references figures.

claim: The presence of DPP6 or DPP10 subunits in the macromolecular complex of Kv4 channels is a requirement in conferring high AmmTx3 sensitivity.
source: Interestingly, the presence of DPP6 or DPP10 subunits in the macromolecular complex of Kv4 channels is a requirement in conferring high AmmTx3 sensitivity (Maffie et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work establishing this requirement.

claim: The majority of mouse hippocampal CGE-NGFC IKA is most likely mediated via a combination of Kv4.2 and Kv4.3 containing channels.
source: Taken together the combined molecular, physiological and pharmacological approach demonstrate that the majority of mouse hippocampal CGE-NGFC IKA which strongly influences intrinsic excitability of this IN subtype, is most likely mediated via a combination of Kv4.2 and Kv4.3 containing channels.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings from multiple experimental approaches to support this conclusion.

claim: Bath application of AmmTx3 had no significant effect on either the amplitude of EPSCs or paired pulse ratio.
source: Bath application of AmmTx3 had no significant effect on either the amplitude of EPSCs or paired pulse ratio, whereas a marked significant increase in the depolarization elicited by the same EPSCs when monitored as EPSPs in current clamp (Figure 7A–D).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental observations with pharmacological manipulation and statistical analysis, and references figures.

claim: Bath application of AmmTx3 produced a marked significant increase in the depolarization elicited by EPSCs when monitored as EPSPs in current clamp.
source: Bath application of AmmTx3 had no significant effect on either the amplitude of EPSCs or paired pulse ratio, whereas a marked significant increase in the depolarization elicited by the same EPSCs when monitored as EPSPs in current clamp (Figure 7A–D).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental observations with pharmacological manipulation and statistical analysis, and references figures.

claim: Pharmacological modulation of Kv4 mediated IKA conductance in NGFCs produces EPSP amplification facilitating the extent of temporal summation of excitatory afferent inputs onto NGFCs, independent to any changes in presynaptic release probability or postsynaptic glutamate receptor function.
source: These data demonstrate that pharmacological modulation of Kv4 mediated IKA conductance in NGFCs alone, produces EPSP amplification facilitating the extent of temporal summation of excitatory afferent inputs onto NGFCs, independent to any changes in presynaptic release probability or postsynaptic glutamate receptor function.
evidence: The manuscript interprets experimental findings to support this conclusion about the mechanism.

claim: In 10 out of 17 NGFCs tested, an increase in action potential output in response to synaptically evoked EPSPs was clearly evident after STP-SE induction.
source: Electrical stimulation was recommenced at the same intensity as that used during baseline. In 10 out of 17 NGFCs tested, an increase in action potential output in response to synaptically evoked EPSPs was clearly evident (Figure 7G,H).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific numerical data from experimental observations and references figures.

claim: The potentiation of EPSP-spike (E-S) coupling possessed a similar mean duration to that seen in increased intrinsic excitability upon somatic depolarization following a single round of conditioning APs.
source: This potentiation of EPSP-spike (E-S) coupling possessed a similar mean duration to that seen in increased intrinsic excitability upon somatic depolarization following a single round of conditioning APs indicating similar underlying mechanisms (Figure 7H vs. Figure 2G; 63 ± 11 s vs. 77 ± 23 s for duration of STP-SE and E-S coupling potentiation, respectively; n = 10, 37; p=0.9; Mann-Whitney U -Test).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific numerical data from experimental observations with statistical analysis and references figures.

claim: A small but significant decrease in sEPSC amplitude after the 4th BF episode (post-BF4) was noted.
source: Interestingly, a small but significant decrease in sEPSC amplitude after the 4th BF episode (post-BF4) was noted, however, this would in fact negatively impact any potentiation noted and serve to minimize heightened E-S coupling.
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental observations with statistical analysis.

claim: No significant changes in sEPSC frequency or tau decay were observed following induction of multiple BF episodes.
source: In addition, no significant changes in sEPSC frequency or tau decay were observed (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental observations with statistical analysis and references figures.

claim: Analyses of spontaneous EPSCs following induction of STP-SE confirm a modulation of intrinsic properties as the main underlying cause for the increased E-S coupling observed.
source: Together analyses of spontaneous EPSCs following induction of STP-SE confirm a modulation of intrinsic properties as the main underlying cause for the increased E-S coupling observed.
evidence: The manuscript interprets experimental findings to support this conclusion about the mechanism.

claim: BF typically requires protracted periods of action potential activity.
source: However, induction of barrage firing typically requires protracted periods of action potential activity (Sheffield et al., 2011; Suzuki et al., 2014) (but see Wang et al., 2015; Yoshida and Hasselmo, 2009) questioning the exact physiological circumstances under which it manifests.
evidence: The manuscript cites prior studies that have characterized the induction requirements for BF.

claim: The operational role of BF in normal brain function remains unclear.
source: Its operational role in normal brain function therefore remains unclear, although it has been postulated to constitute a mechanism for driving network oscillations (Rózsa et al., 2017), an important function of IN subclasses including NGFCs (Capogna, 2011; Overstreet-Wadiche and McBain, 2015; Pelkey et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges uncertainty and cites prior work proposing potential roles.

claim: BF has been proposed to constitute a homeostatic, dampening mechanism during prolonged epochs of circuit over excitation such as those that occur during epilepsy.
source: From a pathological standpoint, it has been proposed to constitute a homeostatic, dampening mechanism during prolonged epochs of circuit over excitation such as those that occur during epilepsy (Elgueta et al., 2015; Suzuki et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior studies that have proposed this pathological role.

claim: Human NGFCs demonstrate a heightened basal excitability when compared to rodent.
source: In agreement with a previous study (Poorthuis et al., 2018), our observations demonstrate a heightened basal human NGFC excitability when compared to rodent (Figure 2C; open black vs.s open orange circles).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental observations and cites prior work showing similar findings.

claim: NGFCs in control non-human primate brain demonstrate a similar heightened basal excitability to human NGFCs.
source: Although we procured human tissue from brain regions distal to the epilepsy focal point that was deemed non-pathological (see Materials and methods for details), we cannot discount possible modulation of neuronal function precipitated by patient treatment regimens. However, NGFCs in control non-human primate brain also demonstrate a similar heightened basal excitability (Povysheva et al., 2007) suggesting that this indeed reflects an evolutionary distinction.
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work showing similar findings in non-human primates.

claim: It is highly unlikely that either disease progression and/or drug treatment in humans would result in species mirroring in the propensity to express activity-dependent modulation.
source: Nevertheless, regardless of differences in basal excitability and their underlying reasons, our data clearly demonstrate both mouse and human NGFCs to undergo essentially similar intrinsic plasticity. It is highly unlikely that either disease progression and/or drug treatment in humans would result in species mirroring in the propensity to express such an activity-dependent modulation described.
evidence: The manuscript provides reasoning based on the similarity of findings across species.

claim: The intrinsic plasticity demonstrated by human NGFCs are not a consequence of disease state and/or drug regimens.
source: Therefore, although the ability of non-human primate NGFCs to undergo STP-SE (and BF) is unknown, we are confident that the intrinsic plasticity demonstrated by human NGFCs are not a consequence of disease state and/or drug regimens.
evidence: The manuscript provides reasoning based on the similarity of findings across species and comparison to non-human primates.

claim: Mouse NGFCs express Kv4 and auxiliary subunit transcripts that translates to a functional IKA conductance.
source: In the current study, we show that mouse NGFCs express Kv4 and auxiliary subunit transcripts that translates to a functional IKA conductance.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings from RNAseq and electrophysiological analyses.

claim: IKA can effectively influence delay to spike and action potential threshold resulting in increased intrinsic excitability like that seen in STP-SE.
source: We extend these observations to NGFCs and demonstrate IKA can effectively influence delay to spike and action potential threshold resulting in increased intrinsic excitability like that seen in STP-SE ultimately resulting in enhanced dendritic integration.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes experimental findings showing the effects of IKA modulation.

claim: STP-SE is more readily induced under conditions where IKA is inhibited.
source: This coupled with the fact that STP-SE is more readily induced under conditions where IKA is inhibited points to a potential modulation of this conductance in the expression of intrinsic plasticity described in this study.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes experimental findings showing the effects of IKA inhibition on STP-SE induction.

claim: Additional contributions of other channels expressed along the axodendritic axes (e.g. KCNQ, HCN, ether-a-go-go, SK/BK channels) could contribute to produce the enhanced excitability and E-S coupling described.
source: As such, we cannot presently exclude additional contributions of other channels expressed along the axodendritic axes (e.g. KCNQ, HCN, ether-a-go-go, SK/BK channels), a complex interplay of which, could contribute to produce the enhanced excitability and E-S coupling described here.
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges limitations and speculates about alternative mechanisms.

claim: Examination of available RNAseq data from mouse and human reveals essentially a complete absence of Kcna1 mRNA levels in human IN populations.
source: For example, examination of available RNAseq data from mouse and human via available transcriptomic explorers (Hodge et al., 2019; Krienen et al., 2019) (http://celltypes.brain-map.org/rnaseq/mouse_ctx-hip_smart-seq.; http://celltypes.brain-map.org/rnaseq/human_ctx_smart-seq. ; http://interneuron.mccarrolllab.org/) reveals essentially a complete absence of Kcna1 mRNA levels in human IN populations (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript describes analysis of publicly available RNAseq data and references figures.

claim: Gene expression of Kcnd2, Kcnd3 (and associated auxiliary subunit mRNA) are conserved across evolution.
source: Interestingly, gene expression of Kcnd2, Kcnd3 (and associated auxiliary subunit mRNA; https://portal.brain-map.org/; http://interneuron.mccarrolllab.org/) are conserved across evolution (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript describes analysis of publicly available RNAseq data and references figures.

claim: A direct functional role for Kv4 channels in dictating human NGFC excitability akin to that in mouse remains to be experimentally ascertained.
source: However, a direct functional role for these subthreshold conductances in dictating human NGFC excitability akin to that in mouse remains to be experimentally ascertained.
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges the need for future experimental validation in human tissue.

claim: Dendritic inhibition exerts a strong influence on excitability and electrogenesis in distal pyramidal cell subdomains.
source: At the cellular level, dendritic inhibition exerts a strong influence on excitability and electrogenesis in distal pyramidal cell subdomains (Kepecs and Fishell, 2014; Pelkey et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work establishing this role of dendritic inhibition.

claim: Various behaviors are encoded through the activity and modulation of dendritic targeting INs.
source: Given these critical network roles, it is not surprising that various behaviors are encoded through the activity and modulation of dendritic targeting INs (Cummings and Clem, 2020; Lovett-Barron et al., 2014; Abs et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior studies demonstrating behavioral correlates of dendritic targeting IN activity.

claim: A correlation between the recruitment of inhibition mediated by NDNF-expressing cells and conditioned learning in mice has been demonstrated.
source: Recently, a correlation between the recruitment of inhibition mediated by NDNF-expressing cells (a subpopulation corresponding to NGFCs [Abs et al., 2018; Tasic et al., 2016] and conditioned learning in mice has provided the first description of a link between NGFC function and behavior (Abs et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites a prior study demonstrating this correlation.

claim: The control of dendritic excitability, including that mediated by Kv4 channels, alters the propensity for LTP induction/expression of excitatory afferent input onto pyramidal cells.
source: The control of dendritic excitability, including that mediated by Kv4 channels, alters the propensity for LTP induction/expression of excitatory afferent input onto pyramidal cells (Kim and Hoffman, 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work demonstrating this role of Kv4 channels in LTP.

claim: Mouse NGFCs exhibit Hebbian long-term plasticity (LTP) triggered by Ca2+-influx via NMDA receptor and/or VGCC activation.
source: Interestingly, mouse NGFCs also exhibit Hebbian long-term plasticity (LTP) triggered by Ca2+-influx via NMDA receptor and/or VGCC activation (Mercier et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work demonstrating this form of plasticity in NGFCs.

claim: NGFCs located in superficial regions of cortex and hippocampus are impinged upon via multiple glutamatergic (e.g. thalamic and cortical) and neuromodulatory afferent populations.
source: NGFCs located in superficial regions of cortex and hippocampus are impinged upon via multiple glutamatergic (e.g. thalamic and cortical) and neuromodulatory afferent populations (Abs et al., 2018; Chittajallu et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2010; Mercier et al., 2019) each conveying distinct information.
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple prior studies demonstrating these afferent inputs.

claim: Increased intrinsic excitability occurring in response to the activity of a given specific afferent input can render a second distinct input more efficacious in NGFC recruitment for short- or long-term periods.
source: Thus, it is plausible that increased intrinsic excitability occurring in response to the activity of a given specific afferent input can render a second distinct input more efficacious in NGFC recruitment for short- or long-term periods.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about potential functional implications of the observed plasticity.

claim: CGE-NGFCs are largely derived from an embryonic progenitor pool originating in the caudal ganglionic eminence (CGE).
source: Here, we focused on mouse and human NGFCs that reside in the most superficial regions of cortex and hippocampus. These NGFCs are largely derived from an embryonic progenitor pool originating in the caudal ganglionic eminence (CGE) (Overstreet-Wadiche and McBain, 2015) Pelkey et al., 2017 #55}.
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work establishing the developmental origin of these NGFCs.

claim: Another distinct group of NGFCs (along with the closely related Ivy cells) have been identified particularly in mouse hippocampus and can be delineated based on a distinct developmental origin in the medial ganglionic eminence (MGE).
source: Another distinct group of NGFCs (along with the closely related Ivy cells Overstreet-Wadiche and McBain, 2015; Pelkey et al., 2017 have been identified particularly in mouse hippocampus and can be delineated based on a distinct developmental origin in the medial ganglionic eminence (MGE).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work establishing the developmental origin of these NGFCs.

claim: Recent cross-species transcriptomic analyses have revealed a remarkable expansion (in terms of number relative to the other IN subtypes) of MGE-derived NGFCs that appear in deeper layers of human sensory and associational cortices when compared to equivalent brain regions in mouse.
source: Intriguingly, recent cross-species transcriptomic analyses have revealed a remarkable expansion (in terms of number relative to the other IN subtypes) of MGE-derived NGFCs that appear in deeper layers of human sensory and associational cortices when compared to equivalent brain regions in mouse (Krienen et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites a prior study demonstrating this evolutionary expansion.

claim: Whether the expanded population of MGE-derived cortical NGFC population in humans undergo similar intrinsic property modulation to their CGE counterparts remains to be determined.
source: Whether this expanded population of MGE-derived cortical NGFC population in humans undergo similar intrinsic property modulation to their CGE counterparts described here remains to be determined.
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges the need for future experimental investigation.

claim: Both mouse and human NGFCs possess a remarkably similar propensity to modulate their intrinsic properties in the face of ongoing activity.
source: However, regardless of the exact mechanistic underpinnings, we clearly demonstrate that both mouse and human NGFCs possess a remarkably similar propensity to modulate their intrinsic properties in the face of ongoing activity.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the main finding of the study.

claim: The evolutionary retention of these mechanisms reveals circuit motifs that represent critical facets of human brain function.
source: The evolutionary retention of these mechanisms reveals circuit motifs that represent critical facets of human brain function.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the conservation of plasticity mechanisms across species as indicating functional importance.

claim: This conservation highlights the mouse model as an applicable tool to predict the potential human behavioral correlates dependent on the tuning of inhibition mediated by this subtype of specialized neuron.
source: From a research perspective this conservation highlights the mouse model as an applicable tool (Abs et al., 2018) to predict the potential human behavioral correlates dependent on the tuning of inhibition mediated by this subtype of specialized neuron.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the conservation of plasticity mechanisms as validating the use of mouse models for understanding human brain function.

claim: In every participant, electrophysiological analyses were derived from cortical specimens that lay outside of the seizure onset zone as determined by intracranial recordings and thus deemed electrographically normal.
source: In every participant, our slice electrophysiological analyses were derived from cortical specimens that lay outside of the seizure onset zone as determined by intracranial recordings and thus deemed electrographically normal (see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental approach for human tissue procurement.

claim: NGFCs possess the ability to influence other IN subtypes including each other via chemical (GABA mediated) and electrical (gap junction mediated) modalities.
source: Additionally, NGFCs possess the ability to influence other IN subtypes including each other via chemical (GABA mediated) and electrical (gap junction mediated) modalities (Armstrong et al., 2011; Boldog et al., 2018; Chittajallu et al., 2013; Chu et al., 2003; Oláh et al., 2007; Price et al., 2005; Simon et al., 2005).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple prior studies demonstrating these modes of NGFC influence.

claim: NGFC physiology has been studied in rodents, non-human primates and humans revealing both similar and divergent properties across these species.
source: Interestingly, NGFC physiology has been studied not only in rodents but also in non-human primates and humans revealing both similar and divergent properties across these species (Boldog et al., 2018; Oláh et al., 2007; Poorthuis et al., 2018; Povysheva et al., 2007; Zaitsev et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple prior studies comparing NGFC properties across species.

claim: Only a few reports have described short and long-term plasticity impacting recruitment and activity of mouse NGFCs.
source: However, only a few reports have described short and long-term plasticity impacting recruitment and activity of mouse NGFCs (Li et al., 2014; Mercier et al., 2019) with a conspicuous lack of published evidence demonstrating any such mechanisms in their human counterparts (Rózsa et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior studies and notes the lack of evidence in humans.

claim: There is a conspicuous lack of published evidence demonstrating plasticity mechanisms in human NGFCs.
source: However, only a few reports have described short and long-term plasticity impacting recruitment and activity of mouse NGFCs (Li et al., 2014; Mercier et al., 2019) with a conspicuous lack of published evidence demonstrating any such mechanisms in their human counterparts (Rózsa et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites a prior review noting the lack of evidence in humans.

claim: Amongst the varied IN located in superficial regions of cortical and hippocampal microcircuits, NGFCs in both species were found to be privileged with regard expression of these forms of plasticity.
source: Remarkably, amongst the varied IN located in superficial regions of cortical and hippocampal microcircuits, NGFCs in both species were found to be privileged with regard expression of these forms of plasticity.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes experimental findings showing that NGFCs, but not other INs, express these forms of plasticity.

claim: The data reveal the presence of cellular mechanisms that result in modulation of intrinsic excitability of NGFCs that represent circuit motifs important for human brain function.
source: Together our data reveal the presence of cellular mechanisms that result in modulation of intrinsic excitability of NGFCs that represent circuit motifs important for human brain function.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the main finding and its implications.
